title: Cleaning old paintings
passage:
For much of the twentieth century, conservators treated the yellowed varnish on an old painting as an intruder. Varnish darkens with age. It turns blues toward green and buries the crisp edges a painter worked hard to make. The remedy seemed obvious: remove it and let the original colors speak. Museums that took on ambitious cleanings often unveiled canvases so bright that visitors gasped, and the gasps were taken as proof that something had been recovered.

Yet the idea of an 'original' painting is less stable than it looks. Many painters knew their work would be varnished and mixed their colors with that final, warming layer in mind. Some applied glazes, thin translucent layers of tinted oil or resin, that are chemically hard to tell apart from later varnish. A solvent strong enough to lift centuries of grime may take a glaze with it, and a removed glaze cannot be put back. What the delighted visitor sees, then, may not be the painting as its maker last saw it, but a version no one in the painter's lifetime ever saw.

The defenders of thorough cleaning have a reply, and it is not a foolish one. Leaving discolored varnish in place is also a choice, they argue, and it too puts a modern taste, a fondness for the patina of age, in place of the painter's intention. The brown 'old master' look that collectors once prized was, on this view, an accident of chemistry later mistaken for a style.

Both camps share an assumption I find doubtful: that the conservator's task is to reach a single correct state of the object. A painting is not a message sealed in a bottle, waiting to be read exactly as written. It is a physical thing that has aged, been retouched, trimmed, remounted and looked at by generations whose eyes were trained differently from ours. To pretend that all of this can be peeled away is to treat history as dirt.

What follows is not paralysis but humility. The most defensible conservation is reversible: it uses materials that a future conservator, with better instruments and different questions, could remove without harm. Cleaning should proceed in small tests that are documented and made public, so that viewers understand they are looking at an interpretation. The gasp in the gallery is a pleasure, but it is not evidence.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
qs.a: Since a painting's original state is uncertain, conservation should be cautious, reversible and openly interpretive
w: Discolored varnish should always be removed so that viewers can finally see a painting's true, original colors
Leaving old varnish in place is the only way to respect what a painter intended a finished work to look like
Museums should stop cleaning old paintings entirely until stronger and more precise solvents can be developed
qs.e: The author rejects both full cleaning and leaving varnish as the 'correct' state, then argues for humility: reversible methods, small tests and public documentation. The passage explicitly says the conclusion is 'not paralysis.'

qs.q: The author mentions visitors' gasps in both the first and last paragraphs most likely in order to:
qs.a: Suggest that a strong reaction to a cleaned painting does not prove the cleaning was faithful
w: Show that the public strongly supports thorough cleaning of old paintings
Argue that museums should display only paintings that have not been cleaned
Prove that cleaned paintings are more beautiful than uncleaned ones are
qs.e: The first paragraph says gasps were 'taken as proof,' and the last says the gasp 'is not evidence.' The repetition frames the author's skepticism about treating delight as confirmation.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward the defenders of thorough cleaning is best described as:
qs.a: Respectful but ultimately unconvinced
w: Openly contemptuous of their view
Fully persuaded by their argument
Indifferent to the cleaning debate
qs.e: The author calls their reply 'not a foolish one' but then says both camps share a 'doubtful' assumption.

qs.q: Which practice would the author most likely support?
qs.a: Applying a removable new varnish after small, documented test cleanings
w: Repainting faded areas to match the colors the artist described in surviving letters and notes
Removing all later retouching so that only the artist's own brushwork remains on the canvas
Leaving every painting untouched, since any cleaning would amount to an interpretation
qs.e: The final paragraph endorses reversible materials and documented small tests. Repainting and stripping all history assume a single correct state, which the author doubts.

title: What libraries are for
passage:
Ask a city council how its public library is doing and you will likely hear a number: books loaned, perhaps, or visits per year. Circulation figures have the virtue of being easy to count, and in an era of tight budgets, what can be counted tends to be what gets funded. When loans decline, as they have in many systems since the spread of e-books and streaming, the conclusion seems to write itself: the library is a declining institution, a warehouse for an outdated medium.

This reasoning mistakes the library's most visible function for its most important one. The sociologist Ray Oldenburg coined the term 'third place' for settings outside home and work, such as cafés, barbershops and pubs, where people gather informally and regulars come to know one another. Oldenburg's examples were mostly commercial, and there lies a problem: in a café, you are welcome roughly as long as you are buying. The public library is one of the very few indoor places in a modern city where a person may sit for hours, warm and dry, without spending money or explaining why they are there.

That fact explains who uses libraries most heavily: students without a quiet room at home, job seekers without internet access, older people who live alone, parents with small children on a cold afternoon. These visitors may never borrow a book. In the ledger of circulation statistics they are invisible; in the life of a neighborhood they are much of the point.

None of this means the library's traditional mission is obsolete. Reading remains at its center, and a library that abandoned books would lose the quiet seriousness that sets it apart from a shopping mall. But planners should stop treating everything other than lending as a distraction to be tolerated. Seating, restrooms, power outlets and long opening hours are not extras on top of the library's work; for many patrons, they are the work.

The harder question is whether a society that measures institutions by output can learn to value one whose chief product is unhurried presence. The answer will be decided less by librarians than by the people who write their budgets.

qs.q: The author's central claim is that:
qs.a: Libraries are valuable largely as free public spaces, which circulation figures don't capture
w: Libraries should replace most of their books with digital media in order to stay relevant
Falling circulation figures show that public libraries have become declining institutions
Cafés and barbershops serve the same social purpose as libraries and could replace them
qs.e: The author argues that counting loans misses the library's role as a free place to be, while still keeping reading at its center.

qs.q: The author refers to Ray Oldenburg mainly in order to:
qs.a: Introduce a useful concept, then show how libraries differ from his examples
w: Prove that cafés are more important to neighborhoods than libraries
Argue that every third place should operate as a commercial business
Show that sociologists have largely ignored libraries in their work
qs.e: The author borrows 'third place' but points out that Oldenburg's examples require spending money, which makes the library unusual.

qs.q: Based on the passage, the author would most likely agree that a library that got rid of all its books would:
qs.a: Lose part of what makes it different from commercial spaces
w: Serve job seekers and students better than before
Become a more successful third place for regulars
Raise its circulation figures by drawing new visitors
qs.e: The fourth paragraph says abandoning books would cost the library its 'quiet seriousness' that sets it apart from a mall.

qs.q: A city plans to cut library opening hours but keep the book budget the same, pointing to steady loan numbers. The author would most likely respond that the plan:
qs.a: Ignores the patrons who depend on the library as a place to be, not just a source of loans
w: Is reasonable, because lending books is the library's main purpose and it is protected
Should cut the book budget instead, since books are less important than open hours
Will raise circulation by concentrating borrowers into fewer, busier opening hours
qs.e: The author lists long opening hours among the things that 'are the work' for many patrons. Judging the library only by loans is exactly the mistake the passage criticizes.

title: Faithful or beautiful
passage:
There is an old joke among translators that a translation, like a lover, can be either faithful or beautiful, but not both. The joke is unkind in several directions at once, and it is also, I think, wrong about translation, though not for the reason usually given.

The usual rebuttal holds that a skilled translator can achieve both fidelity and beauty with enough effort. This underestimates the difficulty. A poem's sound is not decoration laid over its meaning; it is woven into it. When a line in one language rhymes, the rhyme binds two words together and asks the reader to hear them as related. Carry the meanings into another language and the bond usually snaps, because the matching words no longer chime. The translator may find a new rhyme, but it will join different words and suggest a different relationship. Something has been invented, not preserved.

Where the joke goes wrong is in its picture of fidelity. It imagines the original poem as a fixed set of meanings, so that a translation is faithful to the extent that it reproduces them one by one. But readers of the original do not receive a list of meanings; they go through an experience in which sense, sound, rhythm and expectation interact. A word-for-word version that keeps every dictionary meaning while turning music into prose is faithful to an inventory, not to the poem.

Seen this way, the translator's choice is not between loyalty and betrayal but among different kinds of loyalty. One may keep the poem's argument and let its music go; one may rebuild the music and let some of the argument shift; one may produce a version so plain that it sends the reader back to the original. Each is honest if it says what it is doing. The dishonest translation is the one that pretends to have lost nothing.

This is why readers who cannot read the original are often best served by more than one translation. Each shows a different face of the poem, and the poem itself appears, if anywhere, in the space between them.

qs.q: According to the author, the main flaw in the old joke is that it:
qs.a: Treats faithfulness as reproducing a list of meanings
w: Underestimates how skilled good translators really are
Assumes that poems cannot be translated at all
Places too much value on the sound of a poem's lines
qs.e: The third paragraph says the joke 'goes wrong' in its 'picture of fidelity,' which imagines a poem as a fixed set of meanings.

qs.q: The discussion of rhyme in the second paragraph mainly serves to:
qs.a: Show why some loss in translating poetry cannot be avoided
w: Prove that rhyming poems should not be translated
Argue that rhyme matters less than meaning
Show that skilled translators can preserve every rhyme
qs.e: The author uses rhyme to argue against the 'usual rebuttal.' A new rhyme invents a different relationship, so something is always lost.

qs.q: Which would the author most likely consider a dishonest translation?
qs.a: One whose preface claims it captures the original poem completely
w: A plain prose version that admits it drops the poem's music
A version that rebuilds the rhymes and notes where the meaning shifts
A literal version meant to send readers back to the original
qs.e: The author says each approach is honest 'if it says what it is doing,' and that the dishonest translation 'pretends to have lost nothing.'

qs.q: A student who can't read Russian wants to study a famous Russian poem. Based on the passage, the author would most likely advise the student to:
qs.a: Compare several translations that take different approaches
w: Find the single most literal, word-for-word translation
Read only the translation with the most faithful rhymes
Avoid translations entirely and read a prose summary instead
qs.e: The last paragraph says readers are often 'best served by more than one translation,' because the poem appears 'in the space between them.'

title: Railway time
passage:
Before the railways, every town kept its own time. Noon was when the sun stood highest over the local church, and a traveler moving east or west could find that the clocks of neighboring towns disagreed by several minutes. Few people minded, because few people traveled fast enough for the difference to matter.

Railways changed that. A timetable that listed departures in a dozen local times invited confusion and, worse, collisions on single-track lines. Railway companies began to run on a single standard time, and towns along the lines gradually set their public clocks to match. What began as an operating convenience became, within a few decades, the way ordinary life was scheduled. Standard time zones, adopted widely in the late nineteenth century, made official what the railways had already made routine.

It is tempting to tell this as a story of simple progress: confusion replaced by coordination. But historians of labor have pointed to another side. The factory, like the railway, depended on synchronized human activity, and the factory clock became the instrument by which workers' time was measured, bought and disciplined. Fines for lateness, bells that marked the start and end of shifts, and later the punch clock all taught a new habit: experiencing the day as a series of units that belonged to someone else. Older rhythms of work, organized around tasks (the harvest brought in, the cloth woven), gave way to work organized around hours.

The point is not that clock time was imposed by villains. Coordinated time made possible things almost everyone came to value, from reliable trains to scheduled medical appointments. The point is that a technical standard is never only technical. It reorganizes who waits for whom, whose time counts as money, and what it means to be 'on time.'

Today, as phones quietly update themselves across time zones and work increasingly spills beyond fixed hours, the settlement reached in the industrial era is shifting again. Whether the result frees time or claims more of it is not something the technology will decide by itself.

qs.q: The main purpose of the passage is to:
qs.a: Argue that standardized time brought real benefits and new control over people's time
w: Explain how railway engineers calculated the boundaries of the first time zones
Argue that clock time was forced on workers by greedy and deliberate factory owners
Show that local solar time was more accurate and more useful than standard time
qs.e: The author grants the benefits ('not imposed by villains') while stressing that standards reorganize power over time.

qs.q: The author mentions work 'organized around tasks' in order to:
qs.a: Contrast an older rhythm of work with work measured in hours
w: Show that farmers resisted the arrival of the railways
Explain how factory owners decided on shift lengths
Argue that task-based work was more productive than shifts
qs.e: Task-based rhythms (finishing a harvest) are the 'before' picture. Clock-measured shifts are the 'after.'

qs.q: The claim that 'a technical standard is never only technical' is supported in the passage mainly by:
qs.a: The example of factory clocks being used to measure and discipline workers
w: The fact that neighboring towns' clocks once disagreed by several minutes
The danger of collisions on single-track lines with mixed timetables
The way phones now update themselves automatically across time zones
qs.e: The factory example shows a timekeeping standard shaping power relationships, not just coordination.

qs.q: A company drops fixed shifts and instead tracks employees' online activity minute by minute, at any hour. The author would most likely view this as:
qs.a: A new version of the control over workers' time that factory clocks once provided
w: A return to the older, task-based rhythms of preindustrial work
A purely technical change that has no real social consequences
Proof that new technology always gives workers more free time
qs.e: The final paragraph raises the question of whether new technology 'claims more' of people's time. Constant tracking extends the factory clock's discipline beyond fixed hours.

title: Keeping ruins as ruins
passage:
A ruin is, strictly speaking, a failure. A roofless abbey no longer shelters monks; a broken aqueduct carries no water. Yet societies spend considerable sums to keep such failures exactly as they are, stabilizing a wall so that it will neither fall nor be rebuilt. The arrangement would puzzle anyone who thought buildings existed only to be used.

In the nineteenth century, this puzzle divided architects. The French restorer Eugène Viollet-le-Duc held that restoration could return a building to a state of completeness, even one that, as he openly admitted, might never have existed at any single moment. His English critic John Ruskin saw such work as a kind of lie: a restored building, he thought, destroyed the very marks of age and labor that made it worth keeping, replacing a true old thing with a false new one.

Modern heritage practice has largely sided with Ruskin, though for reasons he might not recognize. Where Ruskin spoke of reverence, conservators now speak of evidence. A stone worn by centuries of feet is a record of use; a repair in mismatched brick is a record of a later community's priorities. Rebuild the wall and you erase the archive.

Still, the ruin's appeal is not only documentary. Standing in a broken nave, open to the sky, visitors often describe a feeling that is hard to name, something between melancholy and relief. The ruin shows that even great works pass, and in doing so it relieves the present of having to be permanent. A fully restored cathedral says 'this endures'; a ruin says 'this, too, will end,' and some people find that the more comforting message.

If so, the decision to preserve a ruin as a ruin is not a compromise between using a building and abandoning it. It is a choice to keep a particular kind of meaning available, one that a complete building, however beautiful, cannot offer.

qs.q: Which statement best summarizes the author's argument?
qs.a: Ruins deserve preserving as ruins because they offer meaning a complete building can't
w: Ruins should be restored so that they can be used again by their communities
Viollet-le-Duc was right that restoration can return a building to completeness
Ruins are valuable only as physical evidence of how buildings were once used
qs.e: The last paragraph states the thesis. The fourth paragraph adds that the ruin's appeal is 'not only documentary,' which rules out the last option.

qs.q: How does the passage describe the relationship between modern heritage practice and Ruskin's views?
qs.a: It reaches the same conclusion as Ruskin but for different reasons
w: It rejects Ruskin's conclusion and favors full restoration instead
It follows Ruskin's reasoning about reverence exactly
It ignores the debate between Ruskin and Viollet-le-Duc entirely
qs.e: Modern practice 'largely sided with Ruskin, though for reasons he might not recognize': evidence rather than reverence.

qs.q: In the third paragraph, 'erase the archive' most nearly means:
qs.a: Destroy the physical traces that record a building's history
w: Throw away the written records kept about a building
Close a historic building to visiting researchers
Lose the original architect's drawings and plans
qs.e: The 'archive' is the worn stone and mismatched repairs, the physical record of use described in the same paragraph.

qs.q: A town debates rebuilding the roof of its ruined abbey so the space can host concerts. The author would most likely:
qs.a: Prefer stabilizing the ruin, since rebuilding would erase its evidence and its meaning
w: Support rebuilding, because buildings exist to be used and concerts would use it
Support rebuilding, as long as the new roof closely matches the original design
Have no preference, since both stabilizing and rebuilding preserve the site
qs.e: The author values the ruin's physical record and its 'this, too, will end' meaning, both of which a new roof would take away.

title: The obligations of a gift
passage:
In an influential essay published in the 1920s, the French anthropologist Marcel Mauss argued that gifts are never truly free. Across the societies he surveyed, a gift created three obligations: to give, to receive and to give back. Refusing a gift could be an insult; failing to return one could cost a person standing. Mauss's point was not that people are secretly calculating, but that exchanging gifts weaves social bonds that buying and selling do not.

The contrast with market exchange is useful. When I buy bread, the transaction is complete when I pay; the baker and I owe each other nothing more, and we can walk away as strangers. That is exactly its advantage: markets let people cooperate without knowing or trusting one another. A gift, by contrast, is designed to be incomplete. It leaves a debt that cannot be settled with exact change, and the relationship lives in that gap.

This is why people are often uncomfortable when a gift is returned too quickly or too precisely. Returning a dinner invitation the next evening, or handing back cash equal to the price of a present, turns the gift into a trade and quietly ends the relationship it was meant to build. Etiquette's insistence on delay and on rough rather than exact equivalence is not mere fussiness; it protects the open account that keeps the bond alive.

Some critics conclude that gift economies are therefore hidden systems of obligation and power, in which generosity is a way of putting others in your debt. There is truth in this; competitive giving can humiliate as well as bind. But the criticism proves less than it seems to. Every relationship involves obligations, and the alternative to being bound to others is not freedom but isolation. The question is not whether gifts create ties but which ties a given society wants to encourage.

Online platforms that let neighbors lend tools or share extra food have learned this the hard way. Those that attach exact prices to every exchange tend to attract efficient strangers; those that leave exchanges loosely reciprocal tend to build communities, and sometimes resentments.

qs.q: According to the passage, Mauss's main claim was that gifts:
qs.a: Create obligations that build social ties
w: Are disguised forms of selfish calculation
Are less efficient than market exchange
Should always be returned at equal value
qs.e: The first paragraph says Mauss's point 'was not that people are secretly calculating,' but that gifts weave bonds through obligation.

qs.q: The example of buying bread mainly serves to:
qs.a: Contrast a complete transaction with a gift that is left deliberately incomplete
w: Show that market exchange is morally inferior to exchanging gifts
Illustrate each of Mauss's three obligations with a familiar case
Explain why bakers often give small gifts to their regular customers
qs.e: The bread purchase ends with no further obligation, which highlights how a gift leaves an open debt where 'the relationship lives.'

qs.q: How does the author respond to critics who see gift economies as hidden systems of power?
qs.a: Partly agrees, but says the criticism overlooks that all relationships involve obligations
w: Fully agrees with them and concludes that people should avoid exchanging gifts
Rejects their criticism completely as having no truth to it whatsoever
Argues that market exchange creates far more power imbalances than gifts do
qs.e: The author grants 'there is truth in this' and then says the criticism 'proves less than it seems,' since the alternative to obligation is isolation.

qs.q: A friend thanks you for a birthday present by immediately handing you cash equal to its price. Based on the passage, this would most likely:
qs.a: Turn the gift into a trade and weaken the bond it was meant to build
w: Strengthen the friendship by settling the debt fairly and quickly
Show that your friend values the relationship more than the gift
Have no effect on the friendship, since the values exchanged are equal
qs.e: The third paragraph gives nearly this exact example: exact, quick repayment 'turns the gift into a trade and quietly ends the relationship.'
